title: Two-Set Representation Function
content: The central object of study: $r_{A,B}(n)$ counts the number of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$, and $a + b = n$. Defined via `Set.ncard` on the set of qualifying pairs. Unlike the one-set case $r_{A,A}(n)$ in Problem #28, the two-set version allows $A \neq B$, which introduces fundamentally new behavior — the ratio condition $a_n/b_n \to 1$ becomes necessary to prevent bounded representations.

title: Sumset Definition
content: The sumset $A + B$ is defined as $\{n \mid \exists a \in A, b \in B, n = a + b\}$. This is the Minkowski sum restricted to natural numbers. The key question is: when $A + B$ covers all large integers, how does the multiplicity of coverage (the representation count) behave?
mathContext: $A + B = \{a + b : a \in A,\, b \in B\}$

title: Two-Set Basis Definitions
content: Two equivalent formulations of 'asymptotic basis': (1) $\exists N_0$ such that $A + B \supseteq [N_0, \infty)$, and (2) $(A+B)^c$ is finite. The equivalence is proved in `isTwoSetBasis_iff`. The second form is more elegant but the first is more constructive — the proof extracts $N_0 = \sup((A+B)^c) + 1$ from the finite complement.
mathContext: $\text{IsTwoSetBasis}(A,B) \iff (A+B)^c \text{ is finite} \iff \exists N_0,\, \forall n \geq N_0,\, n \in A+B$

title: Counting Function
content: The counting function $A(N) = |A \cap [1, N]|$ measures the density of $A$ up to $N$. Implemented by filtering `Finset.Icc 1 N` against membership in $A$. This is the bridge between the 'element-wise' ratio $a_n/b_n \to 1$ and the 'density' ratio $A(N)/B(N) \to 1$. The two formulations are equivalent for infinite sets with increasing enumerations.

title: Asymptotic Ratio Condition
content: The crucial hypothesis distinguishing Problem #1145 from its false generalization: $A(N)/B(N) \to 1$ as $N \to \infty$, expressed via Lean's `Tendsto` and `atTop` filter. An alternative formulation uses the enumerating sequences directly: $a_n/b_n \to 1$. The equivalence is standard but nontrivial — it requires that both sets are infinite and their enumerations are strictly increasing. Without this condition, Ruzsa's counterexample shows the conjecture fails.

title: Basis Equivalence Proof
content: Proves `IsTwoSetBasis A B ↔ IsTwoSetBasis' A B`. Forward direction: if all $n \geq N_0$ are in $A+B$, then the complement is contained in `Finset.range N₀`, hence finite. Reverse: from a finite complement, extract $N_0 = \sup((A+B)^c) + 1$ so no integer $\geq N_0$ lies in the complement. The empty-complement case is handled separately — if $(A+B)^c = \emptyset$, take $N_0 = 0$. Uses `le_csSup` for the bounded-above finite set and `omega` for arithmetic.

title: Finiteness of Representation Pairs
content: A foundational lemma: the set of pairs $(a,b)$ with $a + b = n$ is always finite, because both components are bounded by $n$. The proof embeds this set into the product $[0,n) \times [0,n)$. This finiteness is essential for `Set.ncard` to give meaningful values — without it, the representation function could be ill-defined.
mathContext: $\{(a,b) \in A \times B : a+b=n\} \subseteq [0,n) \times [0,n)$, which is finite.

title: Positivity of Representation Count
content: If $n \in A + B$, then there exists at least one pair $(a,b)$ with $a + b = n$, so $r_{A,B}(n) \geq 1$. The proof constructs a witness pair from the sumset membership, shows the pair set is nonempty, then applies `Set.ncard_pos` (which requires the finiteness lemma). This is the converse direction of the observation that $r_{A,B}(n) = 0$ iff $n \notin A + B$.

title: Monotonicity of Representation Function
content: Enlarging either set can only increase the representation count: if $A \subseteq A'$ and $B \subseteq B'$, then $r_{A,B}(n) \leq r_{A',B'}(n)$. Proved by `Set.ncard_le_ncard` applied to the subset inclusion of pair sets. This monotonicity is used implicitly in arguments about lower bounds — any lower bound on $r_{A,B}(n)$ automatically applies to supersets.

title: Vanishing for Small Arguments
content: When $n < \min(A) + \min(B)$, no pair can sum to $n$, so $r_{A,B}(n) = 0$. The proof shows the pair set is empty by deriving a contradiction from any alleged pair via `omega`. Combined with positivity, this cleanly characterizes where the representation function can be nonzero.

title: The Erdős–Sárközy Conjecture
content: The heart of the formalization: the open conjecture stated as an axiom. Given infinite $A, B$ with $a_n/b_n \to 1$ and $A + B$ covering all large integers, the representation function $r_{A,B}(n)$ must be unbounded. Formalized as $\forall k,\, \exists n,\, k < r_{A,B}(n)$. This is strictly stronger than the Erdős–Turán conjecture (Problem #28), which is the special case $A = B$. Erdős offered \$500 for Problem #28; this generalization remains wide open with no partial results beyond the $A = B$ case.

title: Reduction to Erdős–Turán
content: The key structural result connecting Problems #1145 and #28: when $A = B$, the two-set representation function equals the one-set version (by `rfl`), and the ratio condition $a_n/b_n \to 1$ holds trivially because $a_n/a_n = 1$ for all $n$ (via `div_self` once the counting function is shown positive). The proof of `hasAsymptoticRatio_self` is the interesting part — it requires showing $A(N) > 0$ for large $N$, which uses the infinitude of $A$ to find an element $a \in A$ with $a > 0$, then filters to show the counting function is positive for all $N \geq a$.
mathContext: $A = B \Rightarrow r_{A,A}(n) = r_{A,B}(n)$ and $\frac{A(N)}{A(N)} = 1$ for $N$ large. Hence #1145 $\Rightarrow$ #28.

title: Ruzsa's Binary Digit Construction
content: Ruzsa's elegant counterexample from Problem #331: define $A$ as numbers whose binary expansion has nonzero digits only in even positions, and $B$ as numbers with nonzero digits only in odd positions. Then every natural number has a unique representation $a + b$ with $a \in A, b \in B$ (binary digits interleave). This gives $A + B = \mathbb{N}$ with $r_{A,B}(n) = 1$ for all $n \geq 1$. Crucially, $|A \cap [1,N]| \sim \sqrt{N}$ and $|B \cap [1,N]| \sim \sqrt{2N}$, so $a_n/b_n \to 1/\sqrt{2} \neq 1$.
mathContext: $A = \{\sum a_i 4^i\}$, $B = \{\sum b_i 2 \cdot 4^i\}$. Each $n$ has unique binary split: even-position bits to $A$, odd-position bits to $B$.

title: Axiomatized Ruzsa Properties
content: Six axioms encode the known properties of Ruzsa's construction: infinitude of both sets, unique representations, bounded representation function ($r = 1$), basis property ($A + B$ covers all large integers), and failure of the ratio condition. These could in principle be proved from the explicit definitions of `ruzsaA` and `ruzsaB`, but the proofs would require extensive binary arithmetic reasoning. The axiomatization is faithful — each property is a theorem about the concrete construction.

title: Necessity of the Ratio Condition
content: The formalization's most substantive proved theorem: the ratio condition $a_n/b_n \to 1$ is **necessary** for the conjecture. The proof assembles Ruzsa's construction as a witness — infinite $A, B$ forming a basis, with $\lnot(a_n/b_n \to 1)$, yet $r_{A,B}(n) \leq 1$ for all $n$. The bound $C = 1$ is established by case-splitting on $n \geq 1$ (using `ruzsa_rep_bounded`) versus $n = 0$ (showing the pair set has at most one element via subset inclusion into a singleton). This makes precise exactly where the boundary lies between the true conjecture and its false generalization.
mathContext: $\exists A, B: A^\infty \wedge B^\infty \wedge \text{IsTwoSetBasis}(A,B) \wedge \lnot(a_n/b_n \to 1) \wedge \forall n,\, r_{A,B}(n) \leq 1$

title: Average Representation Growth
content: Two axiomatized results on average behavior. First, a counting identity: $\sum_{n \leq N} r_{A,B}(n) \geq A(N) \cdot B(N) - \text{error}$, which follows from double counting — each pair $(a,b)$ with $a \leq N$ and $b \leq N$ contributes to $r_{A,B}(a+b)$. Second, if both sets have density $\gg \sqrt{N}$ (the minimal density for a basis), then the average representation $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n \leq N} r_{A,B}(n) \to \infty$. This shows the conjecture is about the **maximum**, not the average — the average already grows.
mathContext: $\sum_{n=0}^{N} r_{A,B}(n) \geq A(N) \cdot B(N) - O(A(N) \cdot B(N))$. If $A(N), B(N) \gg \sqrt{N}$, the average $\to \infty$.

title: Grekos Partial Result
content: An axiomatized partial result due to Grekos, Haddad, Helou, and Pihko: under the full hypotheses of Problem #1145, one can show $r_{A,B}(n) \geq 6$ infinitely often. This is far from the conjecture (which demands unboundedness), but it is the best known unconditional lower bound. The result extends earlier work on the $A = B$ case, where Erdős and Fuchs showed the representation function cannot be eventually constant.

title: Symmetry via Pair-Swap Bijection
content: Proves $r_{A,B}(n) = r_{B,A}(n)$ by constructing an explicit bijection $(a,b) \mapsto (b,a)$ between the pair sets. The proof rewrites the $A$-side pair set as the image of the $B$-side pair set under the swap map, then applies `Set.ncard_image_of_injective`. Injectivity of the swap is shown by component-wise equality. This commutativity is not merely cosmetic — it means the conjecture's truth is symmetric in $A$ and $B$.
prerequisites: image of a set under a function

title: Vanishing for Large Arguments
content: When $A, B \subseteq [0, N]$ are both bounded, $r_{A,B}(n) = 0$ for $n > 2N$. This is the 'upper' companion to the 'lower' vanishing lemma: the representation function is supported on $[\min(A)+\min(B),\, \max(A)+\max(B)]$. For infinite sets the support is unbounded above, but for finite truncations this gives a clean support bound. Useful in finite combinatorial arguments and for bounding sums.
